Approximately 11,476,703 shares changed hands during trading, a decline of 36% from the average session volume of 17,799,492 shares. The stock had previously closed at $178.23. HSBC reiterated a "hold" rating and set a $90.00 target price on shares of ExxonMobil in a research note on Friday, September 25th. Zacks Research upgraded ExxonMobil from a "hold" rating to a "strong-buy" rating in a research note on Monday. Jefferies Financial Group raised their price target on ExxonMobil from $184.00 to $200.00 and gave the company a "buy" rating in a report on Monday, August 17th. One equities research analyst has rated the stock with a Strong Buy rating, eleven have issued a Buy rating and thirteen have given a Hold rating to the company's stock. The company's 50-day simple moving average is $165.33 and its 200-day simple moving average is $154.89. The company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.12, a current ratio of 1.13 and a quick ratio of 0.85. The stock has a market capitalization of $759.46 billion, a price-to-earnings ratio of 23.58, a P/E/G ratio of 0.89 and a beta of 0.21. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM - Get Free Report) last posted its earnings results on Friday, July 31st. The firm had revenue of $114.53 billion during the quarter, compared to analyst estimates of $109.94 billion. ExxonMobil had a net margin of 8.88% and a return on equity of 13.14%. During the same period in the previous year, the company posted $1.64 EPS.  Research analysts forecast that ExxonMobil Corporation will post 13.63 earnings per share for the current fiscal year. The firm also recently announced a quarterly dividend, which was paid on Thursday, September 10th. Stockholders of record on Monday, August 17th were issued a dividend of $1.03 per share. The ex-dividend date of this dividend was Monday, August 17th. This represents a $4.12 annualized dividend and a dividend yield of 2.2%. ExxonMobil's dividend payout ratio (DPR) is currently 53.02%. title: Chevron vs. ExxonMobil: Which Stock Has the Edge at 52-Week Highs? - TradingView
content: Energy giants Chevron Corporation CVX and ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM are attracting investor attention as their shares approach 52-week highs. CVX trades at $226.68, near its 52-week high of $229.04, while XOM changes hands at $178.23 against a high of $180.31. Rising crude prices have supported the stock’s recent gains, with Brent crude surging above $110 per barrel. Both companies benefit from oil and gas production, refining operations and disciplined capital allocation. However, buying near yearly peaks calls for examining whether operational improvements justify continued optimism. Their respective exposure to Guyana, the Permian Basin and downstream markets offers a common basis for comparing production growth, cash generation, operating efficiency and shareholder rewards. Chevron’s appeal centers on its enlarged upstream portfolio following the Hess acquisition. Second-quarter 2026 worldwide production reached 4.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, rising 20% year over year, aided by legacy Hess assets and growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America. Management expects full-year output of 3.98 million to 4.10 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. Its Guyana exposure also provides high-margin oil growth opportunities into the next decade. Cost discipline is another advantage. CVX achieved $1.5 billion in annualized Hess-related synergies, exceeding its original goal, while securing $3 billion in annual structural savings since 2024. These efforts can protect margins when commodity prices retreat. The company also expects to spend 25% less capital per barrel of oil equivalent in its U.S. shale and tight operations this year than last year, indicating stronger capital productivity. Chevron’s financial flexibility supports its investment appeal. It generated $22.6 billion in operating cash flow and $18.1 billion in free cash flow during the second quarter, while reducing total debt by $8.4 billion. A quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share and continued repurchases reinforce its shareholder-return focus. Moreover, a 20-year agreement to supply 2.67 gigawatts of power to a Microsoft data center creates an additional avenue for monetizing natural gas demand. Recent portfolio moves add promise and uncertainty. Agreements in Venezuela contemplate more than $7 billion of joint-venture investment over five years, with ambitions to more than double production to approximately 600,000 barrels daily. Separately, planned changes to Hess Midstream arrangements aim to halve Bakken unit midstream costs, although Chevron anticipates a substantial one-time accounting loss. Political exposure, execution risks and commodity sensitivity remain important considerations near the stock’s high. ExxonMobil brings greater operating scale and a broad portfolio spanning upstream production, fuels, chemicals and specialty products. Its second-quarter output totaled 4.51 million oil-equivalent barrels daily, despite Middle East disruptions. Production in the Permian exceeded 1.8 million barrels daily, and management sees a 9% compound annual growth trajectory there through 2030. In Guyana, the next floating production vessel is scheduled to add 250,000 barrels of daily capacity, reinforcing future supply growth. ExxonMobil’s integrated operations provide another differentiator. Record second-quarter diesel production demonstrated the value of refining capacity when supplies tightened, while chemical margins benefited from regional supply disruptions. Specialty products delivered particularly strong results. This combination gives XOM more ways to capture value beyond crude production, though refining and chemical earnings remain exposed to changes in product spreads and demand. Financial performance also stands out. XOM generated $23.6 billion in operating cash flow and $17.2 billion in free cash flow during the second quarter, alongside $14.7 billion in adjusted earnings. Shareholder distributions totaled $9.4 billion, split between $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in repurchases. Its declared quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share underscores a commitment to recurring cash returns. Efficiency initiatives strengthen ExxonMobil’s longer-term outlook. Cumulative structural cost savings have reached $16.3 billion, providing a platform for further margin improvement as high-value production expands. Still, aggressive capital spending, geopolitical interruptions and dependence on major project execution pose risks. With XOM trading close to its 52-week peak, investors must weigh its operational breadth and growth pipeline against expectations reflected in the share price. Year to date, shares of CVX and XOM have gained 48.8% and 48.2%, respectively. From a valuation perspective — in terms of forward price-to-sales ratio — ExxonMobil is trading at a similar valuation of 1.8X when compared with Chevron’s 1.89X. According to the Zacks Consensus Estimate, CVX’s earnings are set to rise 148.6% in 2026. The same for XOM’s 2026 EPS indicates a year-over-year increase of 95%. Both Chevron and ExxonMobil offer compelling investment opportunities, backed by strong production portfolios, healthy cash flows and consistent shareholder returns, justifying Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) for both companies. ExxonMobil benefits from its larger operating scale, diversified downstream businesses and expanding Permian and Guyana operations. However, Chevron appears better positioned for further upside. Its Hess acquisition, accelerating cost savings, improving capital efficiency and stronger free cash flow provide a solid foundation for future growth. Although both stocks have delivered nearly identical year-to-date gains and trade at comparable forward price-to-sales multiples, Chevron holds a clear advantage in earnings growth prospects. The Zacks Consensus Estimate projects 148.6% earnings growth for CVX in 2026, compared with 95% for XOM, making Chevron the more attractive investment choice. Brent crude prices touched nearly $110 a barrel on Monday as tensions in the Middle East continued to ratchet up. A series of recent escalations, including attacks on commercial ships near the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, and Ukraine’s strike on a Russian refinery, stoked fears about a further constraint in fuel supplies, sending prices higher. Worries continued despite the U.S. government’s efforts to curtail rising prices, including planned fuel releases and changes to U.S. sanctions on Russian imported fuel. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in February, energy prices have been climbing steadily, boosting energy companies. As per Koyfin data, energy stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 by a significant margin in 2026. Exxon Mobil, Chevron, and Marathon Petroleum shares surged to 52-week highs on Monday before closing lower amid the steep climb in oil prices. XOM stock hit an annual high of $179.30 during trading hours on Monday before closing about 0.4% down. CVX stock surged to a 52-week high of $225.67, but ended the session 0.28% lower. MPC stock rallied to a 52-week high of $493.98 during regular trading, but finished the day nearly 1% down. Retail sentiment around XOM, CVX and MPC stocks was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing on Stocktwits. Retail investors in Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) are floating multibillion-dollar buyout scenarios and steep share-price gains after CEO Angelos Stergiou marked the company’s 15th anniversary with a post about its “next chapter.” SLS stock jumped 5% on Monday to $10.49, snapping three straight losing sessions. In his LinkedIn post, Stergiou reflected on Sellas’ growth from a private startup into a public biotech advancing investigational cancer treatments GPS and SLS009. “Reaching 15 years isn't just about celebrating our history; it is about stepping into our next chapter with even greater focus, drive, and resolve,” he said. He acknowledged past setbacks and thanked shareholders, employees and trial participants, while reaffirming the company’s commitment to patients. “Our mission remains deeply personal, and our promise to the patients we aim to serve is steadfast. We look forward, God willing, to the best chapters that are still to be written with GPS and SLS009,” he added. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for SLS slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid a 258% jump in 24-hour message volumes. One user said: “My opinion, Dr. Stergiou’s message was a master-class at reassuring EVERYONE that all is well.” A user also floated a minimum $40 billion valuation. Another user argued for a $50 billion valuation, calling a $247-per-share figure. A separate user proposed a $120 billion buyout scenario and also predicted a share price of $540-plus. Across bullish share-price predictions, including scenarios tied to clinical results, targets ranged from $100 to over $540. Discussing buyout news in case of favorable data, one user said: “If BO news post good data then there’s no stopping this beast (really no explanation required as it could go full berserker mode).” BO means buyout. Another user challenged the lofty valuations and said: “I will be so glad to get out of this ticker when it hits $15 again.” The CEO’s message comes as investors have been searching for potential deal signals in recent months. In June, a filing disclosed changes to executive severance arrangements, including lump-sum payment provisions for Stergiou. For CFO John Burns and chief development officer Dragan Cicic, qualifying departures within one month before or one year after a change of control would trigger 15 months of salary, the annual target bonus, up to 18 months of health-coverage reimbursements and full vesting of unvested equity. Sellas’ conference plans have provided another talking point. The company is listed at Booth 138, with a 20-by-30-foot space, for the Dec.12- Dec.15 American Society of Hematology (ASH) meeting in New Orleans. Major exhibitors include Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Merck, AbbVie and Bristol Myers Squibb. The booth size has fueled speculation about a partnership or acquisition. Currently, investors are awaiting data from Sellas’ two lead programs. The Phase 3 Regal trial is testing GPS, an immunotherapy targeting WT1, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients who achieved a second complete remission following salvage treatment. Its final-analysis process is triggered by 80 deaths. Sellas reported 78 events as of May 11. Reaching 80 precedes database lock, data review and analysis before results are disclosed. The company also expects fourth-quarter topline data from its 80-patient Phase 2 SLS009 study in newly diagnosed AML, including patients with early resistance to azacitidine and venetoclax. SLS009 is also being explored in pancreatic cancer. Preclinical findings from last month showed 17.9% apoptosis (programmed cell death) in a patient-derived tumor model resistant to Daraxonrasib, versus 2.8% with Daraxonrasib alone. Combining the drugs raised apoptosis to 36.5% and necrosis to 30.6%. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. (AVGO) reversed overnight losses to edge up 0.3% late Monday as a 10-year cloud agreement with NTT Docomo did little to ease retail skepticism, with traders seeking a recovery catalyst after CEO Hock Tan’s AI “casino” remarks. AVGO stock rose nearly 2% on Monday to close at $334.59, snapping three straight sessions of losses. Broadcom extended its 2019 deal with Docomo, in which the companies will align their long-term tech roadmaps to advance the private cloud underpinning the Japanese telecom operator’s digital services. The company called it Broadcom Japan’s first “comprehensive” 10-year agreement covering VMware software licenses, technical assistance and maintenance support. Financial terms were not disclosed. VMware Cloud Foundation will be at the core of the infrastructure. The deal targets three priorities: keeping services available during system upgrades, strengthening security and resilience, and accelerating the delivery of new services. Docomo will use the platform to expand capacity and manage traffic spikes, improve security patching and anomaly detection, and run virtual machines and containers on a common platform. Automation across development, testing and releases will help shorten the time needed to introduce new features. The companies also plan to expand AI-driven operations and prepare the infrastructure for future developments, including 6G and IOWN. The agreement comes a week after Tan’s comments at a Singapore panel, where he called capital the biggest constraint on further AI development as Broadcom works through wafer and memory shortages. “A lot of investors have no clue what they're investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino gambling,” Tan said when asked about cheaper AI models, Reuters noted. His remarks addressed investment into the broader AI sector. Tan also acknowledged that Anthropic and OpenAI had shown an ability to generate significant revenue from their latest models deployed for AI personal assistants. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk also subsequently responded, saying, “No crying in the casino,” weighing in on Tan’s concerns about speculative AI investments. (CRWV) shares fell nearly 2% in overnight trading late Monday, putting it on track for a third week of declines amid a selloff in software names. The firm also bought 30,218 shares of CRWV for $1.8 million through the ARK Next Generation Technology ETF (ARKW). The purchase comes as Wall Street and Main Street remain concerned about the company’s ballooning debt levels. CoreWeave reported $35.6 billion in total debt as of June 30, while its second-quarter net interest expense rose to $640 million from $267 million a year earlier. Research and advisory firm Gartner recently said in a report that artificial intelligence infrastructure investments are in danger as concerns over bloated AI capex mount. The firm said that as the commercial duopoly for primary frontier models consolidates around Anthropic and OpenAI, the cash flows to meet that massive computing asset base from neoclouds are not scaling proportionally with upfront costs. Meanwhile, major Wall Street analysts are also taking opposing stances on CoreWeave. MoffettNathanson and BNP Paribas lowered their price targets on CoreWeave, while Goldman Sachs took a more positive outlook. MoffettNathanson slashed CRWV stock’s target to $89 from $107 and kept a ‘Neutral’ rating on the shares, citing its “staggering financial obligations.” BNP Paribas also cut its price target on CoreWeave to $117 from $169 and maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating, according to The Fly. The firm said that it sees a continued deterioration in investor confidence amid its debt obligations. While higher financing costs could contain the company's ability to fund future growth, the shares are "seemingly discounting some liquidity concerns," the analyst reportedly said in a research note. However, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Neutral’ and set a price target of $106, implying upside of more than 73% from its last close. The firm said ongoing volatility in the credit market raises questions about whether CoreWeave can finance its next phase of growth, and at what pace. title: XOM vs. BP: Which Integrated Energy Giant Has the Edge? - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil Holdings CorporationXOM and BP plcBP are two integrated energy giants with promising business prospects, supported by the prevailing strength in crude oil prices. Investors’ strong preferences for both stocks are reflected in the price chart. Over the past year, XOM has jumped 53.6%, outperforming BP’s 42.5% surge. However, the stock price performance does not necessarily establish XOM's superiority over BP as an integrated energy company. Before arriving at an investment conclusion, let's examine the broader upstream business environment, which plays a crucial role in determining the cash flow potential of both energy giants. West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude is again approaching the $100-per-barrel mark, per Oilprice.com. The high prices are being driven by intensifying conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. Energy Information Administration, in its latest short-term energy outlook, projected WTI at $88.21 per barrel this year, higher than $65.40 last year. A highly favorable oil pricing environment is likely to continue supporting ExxonMobil’s exploration and production activities, as is likely for BP, a British energy giant. Importantly, upstream operations generate the majority of earnings for XOM. The company has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing new drilling techniques and artificial intelligence to boost and optimize production volumes at lower cost structures. In Guyana, XOM has made several oil and gas discoveries, further highlighting its solid production outlook. Robust production from both assets has been aiding its top and bottom lines. Breakeven costs are low in both resources. Turning to BP, the British energy major’s production outlook looks bright, as its major projects, expected to begin operations between 2028 and 2030, are moving forward as planned. Once operational, these projects could help BP increase production and generate more cash. Although high oil prices are acting as a tailwind for the businesses of XOM and BP, it is also necessary to analyze the companies’ financial strength to judge how well the two energy majors could weather an unfavorable commodity pricing environment. The debt-to-capitalization of XOM is 13.73%, much lower than BP’s 43.29%. Thus, with significantly lower exposure to debt capital, ExxonMobil Holdings can sail through a tough business environment. BP, although having a relatively higher debt exposure, is also financially sound, as its debt-to-capitalization ratio is not very high. Coming to the valuation, BP stock is currently relatively cheap, as the integrated energy company is trading at a trailing 12-month EV/EBITDA multiple of 3.17x, which is lower than XOM’s 9.91x. In other words, investors are willing to pay a premium price for XOM over BP. The premium valuations reflect XOM’s strong business fundamentals, sound balance sheet and long-term growth prospects. Nevertheless, BP also presents a compelling investment case, given its relatively attractive valuation and the prevailing strength in crude oil prices, which should support its upstream profitability.  moved into sharper market focus as the largest US energy major scheduled its third-quarter results conference call and crude benchmarks traded in triple digits. It remains one of the most-watched Oil and Gas Stocks on Wall Street. The approaching release has pulled the market toward a single question: how a stretch of firmer oil prices has flowed through one of the most closely tracked names in the global energy complex. The timing carries weight because the group sits at the center of the integrated-oil story, spanning the drilling of barrels, the shipping of liquefied natural gas, the running of refineries and the making of chemicals. The company is also a constituent of the NYSE Composite and the Russell 1000. A conference call paired with quarterly figures is routine in form, yet the backdrop of a rallying crude market has given this one added prominence across the energy space. Market attention of this kind tends to build in the days before a major energy release, and the current stretch is no exception. With the barrel firm and the calendar set, the group has moved to the front of the sector conversation, and the figures it reports are expected to serve as an early marker for how the quarter unfolded across the broader complex. Crude has staged a forceful advance, with international and domestic benchmarks pushing into triple-digit territory on a blend of supply fears and firm demand. Each leg higher has drawn attention back toward the companies that pull barrels from the ground, since their earnings move closely with the prevailing price of oil. Market participants have pointed to a tightening of available supply, trimmed output from a producer alliance, and friction along key shipping routes as forces behind the climb. As a member of the S&P 500 and one of the heaviest weights in the energy group, Exxon Mobil has become a reference point whenever the barrel makes a decisive move, and the recent direction has been firmly upward. The strength of the move has also reshaped the tone across trading desks, where the barrel's climb has become a defining feature of the sector story. For a group whose top line tracks the oil price so closely, that momentum has translated into a steady stream of attention, and each fresh move in crude has reinforced the link between the commodity and the stock. The specific development drawing the market's eye is the company's notice that it will host a conference call alongside the release of its third-quarter figures late in the month. The group also flagged, through a routine filing, that sequential movements in oil and natural-gas realizations and in refining margins would shape the quarter against the prior three-month stretch. Such snapshots are customary ahead of a major energy release, giving the market an early read on how price swings across crude, gas and refined products are likely to land. Because the reporting period unfolded against shifting benchmarks, attention has centered on how much of the oil strength reached the bottom line after costs, taxes and the heavy capital the business consumes. The filing-based snapshot is a feature of the way large energy groups communicate ahead of results, offering a measured preview rather than a full account. It lets the market calibrate expectations for the coming figures, and in a quarter marked by shifting benchmarks, that early read has carried more weight than usual across the sector. Exxon Mobil runs an integrated model that stretches across the full length of the energy chain. Upstream, the company drills for and produces crude and natural gas. Midstream and downstream, it moves, refines and markets fuels, while a sizable chemicals arm converts hydrocarbons into plastics and other materials used across manufacturing. That breadth can steady the business through the cycle, because weakness in one link is often offset by strength in another. When crude softens, refining and chemical margins can widen as feedstock costs fall; when crude firms, the upstream arm captures the upside. This balance is a defining feature of the integrated majors and shapes how the market reads each quarterly release. The model also lets the group smooth the heavy capital demands of the business across its various arms, funding drilling in one period and refining upgrades in another. That flexibility, rooted in the scale and breadth of the operation, is part of what distinguishes the largest integrated majors from the narrower producers that populate the rest of the complex. The wider energy complex has been riding the same wave that lifted the barrel, and the gap between realized prices and the cost of pulling hydrocarbons from the ground has widened across much of the space. Tracking the performance of US Oil and Gas Stocks alongside crude itself offers a window into how the rally is reshaping the economics of the group. Many producers entered the stretch with leaner cost structures after years of restraint, so the recent firmness in prices has reached cash generation more cleanly than in earlier cycles. Exxon Mobil stands near the top of that league table by scale, and its integrated footprint gives it exposure across barrels, molecules and refined products that few rivals can match. The health of the broader group also feeds back into how the market reads each individual name, since a firm backdrop lifts confidence in the cash generation of the whole space. When the barrel keeps its ground and costs stay contained, the entire complex tends to draw renewed attention, and the largest names sit at the front of that wave. The company operates an expansive base that spans several continents, anchored by large, long-lived upstream assets and complemented by a global network of refineries and chemical plants. A standout piece of that base sits in the Permian basin of the US southwest, where the group has built one of the largest acreage positions in the region. Alongside onshore shale, the company runs deepwater developments, liquefied natural gas ventures and a chemicals business that ranks among the largest in the world. That mix spreads the group's exposure across geographies, products and currencies, smoothing the impact of any single asset or market stumbling and placing the name among the most watched whenever energy prices move. The geographic spread of the base also means the group is exposed to a wide range of operating conditions, from mature conventional fields to fast-cycle shale wells. Managing that diversity is a defining task for a company of this scale, and the breadth of the footprint is often cited as a source of steadiness through the swings of the commodity cycle. The earnings of an integrated major hinge on the spread between the price at which barrels and molecules are marketed and the cost of producing and processing them. When crude races higher while costs rise only modestly, the upstream spread widens and a larger share of each additional dollar of revenue reaches cash generation. Exxon Mobil, given its enormous production volume, feels that leverage acutely, so even modest moves in the barrel translate into sizable swings in group cash generation. The sensitivity cuts both ways, which is why the market scrutinizes cost guidance and the cadence of capital spending as closely as the headline price. As a member of the S&P 500, the stock also carries broad ownership through index-tracking vehicles, widening the audience for each release. Because the leverage to the barrel is so pronounced, the market pays close heed to how the group manages the cost side of the ledger. Labor, fuel, drilling services and materials all feed into the economics of each barrel, and a group that lets those costs drift can watch a chunk of the price windfall erode before it reaches cash generation. The Permian basin has become a cornerstone of the US upstream story, prized for its stacked layers of oil-bearing rock that allow efficient, repeatable drilling. Exxon Mobil expanded its footprint there through a major combination that lifted it among the largest operators in the region, adding acreage, barrels and operational know-how. Shale output can be scaled up or kept back more quickly than conventional projects, giving operators a lever to respond to shifting prices. The company has emphasized squeezing more barrels from each well while trimming the cost per barrel, a drive that has reshaped the economics of the basin. With crude firm, the Permian position sits at the heart of how the market reads the group's upstream strength. The basin has also become a proving ground for the drilling efficiencies that now define the US onshore business, where longer wells and tighter spacing have lifted the output of each rig. The group's scale there lets it apply those techniques across a vast acreage position, compounding the gains and reinforcing the Permian's place at the core of the upstream story. With cash generation swelling during firmer-price stretches, attention turns to how the company allocates the proceeds. Exxon Mobil has leaned on a long, unbroken record of cash paid out to owners of the stock, pairing a steadily rising dividend with a program that reduces its share count when generation allows. That approach gives the ownership base a direct link to the strength of the barrel while leaving room to fund drilling, refining upgrades and chemical projects. The coming figures are expected to update the market on the balance struck between distributions, the redeployment of cash across the business and the strength of the balance sheet, a mix that has defined the group's capital approach through the recent cycle. The steadiness of that record has long been a defining feature of how the market frames the group, distinguishing it from names with a more variable approach to cash paid out. In a stretch of firm pricing, the market watches whether that steadiness is paired with the discipline to keep spending measured even as cash generation swells. Beyond drilling, the downstream and chemicals arms form a substantial part of the business. Refineries turn crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products, and their margins hinge on the spread between the cost of crude feedstock and the price of refined output. That spread can move independently of the barrel, sometimes cushioning the group when crude softens. The chemicals arm converts hydrocarbons into the building blocks of plastics and countless industrial materials, linking the group to the broader pace of manufacturing and construction. Both arms demand heavy capital and steady operational focus, and the market watches their margins closely as a counterweight to the swings of the upstream business. The crude rally has not unfolded in isolation. Supply fears have been a powerful undercurrent, driven by trimmed output from a producer alliance, friction along critical shipping routes and the threat of trade measures that could crimp available barrels. A firm tone to global demand, led by transport and industry, has reinforced the move. Currency swings add another layer, since crude is priced in dollars and a softer greenback can lift demand from outside the US. Further gains will need a fresh driver, and management named one during a July 31, 2026 call. Executives framed the asset as a turning point for Exxon’s cash. Which project is it, and what has changed there? That project is Exxon’s Guyana development, where the company has now earned back its investment. Management said during the July 31 call that the company fully recovered its $55 billion investment in the region, alongside all operating costs. Under the contract, up to 75% of production can go toward recovering that investment, and management said the remaining production is shared 50-50 with the government of Guyana. Guyana already operates at scale, pumping gross volumes of about 900,000 barrels a day during the second quarter of fiscal 2026. An analyst on the call asked whether the payback means more free cash flow or simply a smaller share of the oil. Management answered that it was “very much an inflection into free cash flow.” In the company’s view, the project has transitioned from paying back its cost to adding to Exxon’s cash. If you have held Exxon Mobil for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not the next catalyst. See how a tax-aware transition works. Guyanese operations fall under Exxon’s Upstream business. That unit generated $102 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025, compared with $324 billion for the entire company. The division also houses the Permian basin, where Exxon set a second-quarter production record of more than 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels a day. A payback event like the one in Guyana ultimately surfaces in cash generation. Exxon posted free cash flow of $17.0 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2026, up from $5.27 billion a year earlier. That single quarter accounted for more than half of the $30.6 billion the company generated over its last four quarters. Speaking about Guyana, management said it expects twice 2025’s level of free cash flow in 2030, and the company is evaluating a ninth FPSO, a floating production ship. Exxon stock finished trading on October 20, 2026, just 0.6% below its highest close of the past year. At that level, the shares traded at 22.7 times earnings over the past four quarters, tracking closely with the 23.0 multiple for the S&P 500. That four-quarter stretch includes the second quarter, which delivered $14.5 billion of the $32.8 billion Exxon earned. The primary doubt is how much of the second quarter’s cash stemmed from oil prices rather than from Guyana. Management said that market prices ran higher than base assumptions, generating more cash sooner. Executives also stated that the conflict in the Middle East affected Exxon’s operations there, and Exxon temporarily lost about 10% of its upstream production in the quarter. The next step in Guyana has a deadline. Exxon’s fifth FPSO, Errea Wittu, set sail toward Guyana in June and remains on track to start up by the end of 2026, management said. That leaves two things to watch: Exxon’s free cash flow in its third-quarter report, expected on or around October 30, 2026, and the start-up of Errea Wittu before the end of 2026.  moved into sharper focus as crude climbed sharply on supply concerns during a busy earnings week, lifting a broad base of energy names before a later easing spurred rotation across the tape. As megacap technology names swung hard through a crowded run of quarterly updates, money leaned toward the oil majors, and the largest integrated producer on the American market drew a fresh bid alongside firmer barrels. Trading desks framed the stretch as a search for ballast while the technology complex churned. Crude sits at the heart of the energy complex, so a sharp climb in the barrel tends to ripple quickly through the producers that pull it from the ground. When oil firms, the output each field delivers fetches a stronger price, lifting the cash a large producer can generate without any change to the barrels it lifts. That leverage to the barrel is a defining feature of the energy arena. A steady climb in crude can lift the reported earnings of an upstream producer faster than the move in oil itself, because the cost of lifting each barrel stays broadly fixed while the sale price rises. The upstream arm finds and produces crude oil and natural gas across a spread of regions, feeding the barrels that anchor the group's earnings. The downstream arm refines that crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products, while the chemical arm converts feedstocks into plastics and specialty materials sold into countless end markets. This integrated design is the hallmark of the business. When crude is strong, the upstream arm drives earnings; when margins on refined fuels widen, the downstream arm carries more weight; and the chemical arm adds a thread tied to broad industrial demand. An integrated energy group captures value at several stages of the chain at after, and that breadth tends to smooth the swings that buffet a pure upstream producer. When crude slides, cheaper feedstock can lift refining and chemical margins, so the downstream arms can cushion a softer barrel, lending the whole group a steadier character across the cycle. That balance cuts the other way too. When crude climbs sharply, as it did this week, the upstream arm shines while refining faces costlier input, yet the combined base still leans toward the firmer barrel. The deepwater development has moved from early finds to steady production, adding a large and growing stream of barrels to the group's base. The Guyana play matters because its barrels come at a competitive cost and from a region where the group holds a commanding position alongside its partners. That offshore engine gives the name a clear growth thread distinct from the mature fields that make up much of the sector. As crude firmed this week, the scale and low cost of the Guyana barrels drew particular attention, since they feed directly into how the market reads the group's expanding production footprint. Alongside its offshore reach, the group holds a deep position in the Permian basin, the vast shale region straddling the American Southwest that has become the engine of domestic oil growth. A large acreage base there feeds a steady stream of barrels that the group can dial up or down with relative speed compared with long-cycle offshore projects. Shale output answers to drilling that can be ramped quickly, giving the group a flexible lever to lean into firmer crude. The Permian barrels sit close to the group's refining and chemical plants along the coast, a proximity that trims transport and knits the upstream and downstream arms more tightly together.
